protocol: NTPv4 (RFC 5905) client request + server response, incl. RFC 5905 App.A symmetric-key MAC

captures.label: A — NTPv4 client request (mode 3), 48 bytes, UDP :123
captures.fieldBreakdown:
0:1:li_vn_mode:0x23 = bits 00|100|011 -> LI=0 (no leap warning), VN=4, Mode=3 (client)
1:1:stratum:0x00 = 0 (unspecified/invalid — normal in a client packet)
2:1:poll:0x06 = i8 +6 -> log2 seconds -> 64 s poll interval
3:1:precision:0xec = i8 -20 -> 2^-20 s ~= 0.95 us local clock precision
4:2:rootDelay.seconds:0x0000 = 0 (NTP short format, upper 16 bits of 16.16)
6:2:rootDelay.fraction:0x0000 = 0 -> root delay 0.000000 s
8:2:rootDispersion.seconds:0x0000 = 0
10:2:rootDispersion.fraction:0x0000 = 0 -> root dispersion 0.000000 s
12:4:referenceId:0x00000000 = none (client, stratum 0, not a KoD)
16:4:referenceTimestamp.seconds:0x00000000 = 0 (never synchronised)
20:4:referenceTimestamp.fraction:0x00000000 = 0
24:4:originTimestamp.seconds:0x00000000 = 0 (client has no prior server packet)
28:4:originTimestamp.fraction:0x00000000 = 0
32:4:receiveTimestamp.seconds:0x00000000 = 0
36:4:receiveTimestamp.fraction:0x00000000 = 0
40:4:transmitTimestamp.seconds:0xee22ea40 = 3995265600 s since 1900-01-01 -> 2026-08-09T12:00:00Z
44:4:transmitTimestamp.fraction:0x4ccccccd = 1288490189/2^32 = 0.3000000000 s -> T1 = 2026-08-09T12:00:00.300000000Z
captures.notes: Byte count verified = 48. CHOSEN LEGAL VALUES: poll=6, precision=-20, and the T1 fraction 0x4ccccccd. RFC 4330 §5 permits a strict SNTP client to zero everything except the first octet and Transmit Timestamp; ntpdate/chrony/w32time additionally fill poll+precision, which is what I emitted. Real clients randomise the low ~26 bits of the T1 fraction as an anti-spoofing nonce; 0x4ccccccd is a legal draw. T1 is the correlation token: the server must echo these 8 bytes verbatim into Origin Timestamp.

captures.label: B — NTPv4 server response (mode 4, stratum 2), 48 bytes, UDP :123

1:1:stratum:0x02 = 2 (secondary server, one hop from a stratum-1 reference)
2:1:poll:0x06 = i8 +6 -> 64 s (server echoes/clamps the client's poll)
3:1:precision:0xe9 = i8 -23 -> 2^-23 s ~= 119 ns
4:2:rootDelay.seconds:0x0000 = 0
6:2:rootDelay.fraction:0x028f = 655/65536 -> root delay 0.0099945068 s
8:2:rootDispersion.seconds:0x0000 = 0
10:2:rootDispersion.fraction:0x0498 = 1176/65536 -> root dispersion 0.0179443359 s
12:4:referenceId:0x81060f1c = IPv4 129.6.15.28 (upstream server; interpretation is stratum-dependent)
16:4:referenceTimestamp.seconds:0xee22e900 = 3995265280 -> 2026-08-09T11:54:40Z
20:4:referenceTimestamp.fraction:0x30000000 = 805306368/2^32 = 0.1875 s -> last sync 2026-08-09T11:54:40.1875Z
24:4:originTimestamp.seconds:0xee22ea40 = verbatim echo of capture A offset 40
28:4:originTimestamp.fraction:0x4ccccccd = verbatim echo of capture A offset 44 -> T1 confirmed
32:4:receiveTimestamp.seconds:0xee22ea40 = 3995265600
36:4:receiveTimestamp.fraction:0x50000000 = 1342177280/2^32 = 0.3125 s -> T2 = 2026-08-09T12:00:00.312500000Z
40:4:transmitTimestamp.seconds:0xee22ea40 = 3995265600
44:4:transmitTimestamp.fraction:0x50200000 = 1344274432/2^32 = 0.31298828125 s -> T3 = 2026-08-09T12:00:00.312988281Z
captures.notes: Byte count verified = 48. CHOSEN LEGAL VALUES: stratum 2, precision -23, refid 129.6.15.28, root delay/dispersion, and the four timestamps. Self-consistency: T1=0.300000, T2=0.312500 (12.5 ms inbound), T3=0.312988 (0.988 ms server processing) — a plausible LAN/WAN exchange. Offset/delay require T4 (local receive instant) which is NOT in the packet: theta = ((T2-T1)+(T3-T4))/2, delta = (T4-T1)-(T3-T2). Root delay is unsigned 16.16 per RFC 5905 §6 'NTP short format' but SIGNED 16.16 per RFC 1305 §3.2 — the same 4 bytes have version-dependent signedness.

captures.notes: Byte count verified = 68 (48 header + 4 key id + 16 digest). Key is ASCII "secret" (73 65 63 72 65 74), key id 1 — chosen legal values. Digest input is 6+48=54 bytes; I computed the MD5 rather than fabricating it. This capture exists specifically to break the grammar: (1) the MAC is a keyed digest whose key is NOT in the message and is a PREFIX, not an HMAC — no `checksum` option expresses that; (2) the presence, algorithm and length of the trailing region is decidable ONLY from the UDP datagram length (48=none, 52=crypto-NAK, 68=MD5, 72=SHA-1, >=76 = extension fields possibly followed by a MAC), and v0 has no `remaining()`.

statefulness:
WHAT NTP ACTUALLY NEEDS FROM §5 — and it is almost the opposite of what §5 offers.

1) Legal-message-per-state: essentially VACUOUS for modes 3/4. NTP client/server is connectionless and stateless by design: there is no connect, no login, no session, no teardown. Every client request is legal at every moment; a server keeps no per-client state at all (that is the whole point — it must answer millions of clients). So `validIn`, `requires` and `conflicts` have nothing to bind to. The state model as drafted is aimed at session protocols and OVER-SERVES here while UNDER-SERVING everything NTP does need. That asymmetry is itself the finding: the model assumes statefulness is about a session, when for NTP it is about a *rate budget*, a *nonce*, and a *decaying measurement*.

2) What must chain: nothing, within basic SNTP. One send, one expect, done — a single request is complete and meaningful on its own. Chaining appears only at the edges: (a) the four-timestamp computation needs T1 remembered from the send step into the expect step (`state.*`, one run — correct scope, but see G9: T1 and T4 are engine events, not document values); (b) NTS (RFC 8915) has a real mandated chain across two transports — NTS-KE over TLS on :4460 yields cookies, then NTP on :123 carries a cookie in an extension field and the response returns a FRESH cookie that replaces the one just spent. That is a self-replenishing one-shot credential pool, which `requires:["login"]` cannot model: the precondition is not "a message succeeded earlier" but "the store holds >=1 unspent cookie", and success consumes one and mints one.

3) What must never combine: mode 6 (control) and mode 7 (private) conversations versus mode 3/4 polling on the same association — and, at the device level, an association is either client, symmetric-active, or broadcast-client, never two at once. `conflicts` is close to right but is scoped "never in the same session", and NTP has no session; the exclusion is per-association and persistent.

4) Where state is CONFIRMED vs PRESUMED:
 - CONFIRMED by the packet itself: the server's stratum, its reference id, its root delay/dispersion, its leap indicator, its precision — all directly observed, at the moment observed.
 - CONFIRMED cryptographically only in capture C: without a MAC or NTS, everything above is merely *asserted by whoever sent the datagram*. The Origin echo (bytes 24-31) is the only off-path defence, and it is a weak one — it confirms "this responder saw my request", not "this is the server I asked".
 - PRESUMED, and the archetypal case for §5's model: the local clock offset. It is a measurement whose error grows continuously from the instant of measurement (dispersion accrues at 15 ppm/s), and the packet ships the decay parameters. §5's `confidence:"likely"` + `ttl:"PT30S"` models a cliff where reality is a ramp (gap G14).
 - PRESUMED and persistent: the negotiated poll interval and version. After one exchange you presume the server still wants poll=6 and still speaks VN=4; you only find out otherwise from the next reply (gap G13).

5) Where you only discover the state is wrong from the NEXT response — this is the richest part, and every instance needs `implies`-style machinery that v0 half-has:
 - LI == 3 in a reply: the server's own clock is unsynchronised. The packet parses perfectly, every timestamp is well-formed, and the answer is worthless. You cannot tell before asking.
 - stratum == 0 in a reply: Kiss-o'-Death. refid is then ASCII, not an address: "RATE" = you are polling too fast, back off (and the demanded poll is in byte 2); "DENY"/"RSTR" = stop contacting this server, permanently. The correct reaction is a persisted deadline or blacklist, not a state label (gap G12). Note the double bind: to know the refid is ASCII you must already have decoded stratum eleven bytes earlier (gap G8).
 - Origin timestamp == 0, or != your T1: the reply is stale, broadcast, or spoofed. Discovered only on receipt, and it must cause a *drop-and-keep-listening*, not a step failure — otherwise a single spoofed packet denies service (gap G11).
 - VN downgraded to 3: your presumed version was wrong; adapt and downgrade future sends.
 - Datagram length 52 with key id 0: crypto-NAK — "your key id or key is wrong". You learn your authentication state is broken purely from the LENGTH of the reply, with no error code anywhere in the bytes. This is state discovered by a *frame size*, which v0 cannot even measure (gap G7).
 - Silence: NTP's most common failure signal. A missing reply is indistinguishable from filtering, loss, a rate-limited server that chose to drop rather than KoD, and a dead host — yet the correct response (exponential backoff, then try another server in the pool) is state. §5 has `onTimeout` on a state but no notion of a per-peer failure budget.

6) Where §5's own listed gaps land here: "no negotiated capability" — CONFIRMED, twice (version, poll). "No sequence-number/window primitive" — CONFIRMED in nonce form: the T1 echo is a one-shot 64-bit nonce with replay semantics, and there is no primitive for mint-remember-verify-retire. "No retransmission + dedup window" — PARTIALLY: NTP itself does not retransmit, but a client polling a pool needs per-peer backoff, which is the same machinery. "No decoder-carried state" — CONFIRMED, in its mildest possible form (refid interpretation keyed on stratum; root-delay signedness keyed on version) which is good news: the fix (G8) is far cheaper than the CoAP-delta case that motivated the entry. "No fragmentation/reassembly", "no modal/exclusive device state", "no two-phase commit" — NOT exercised by NTP; neither confirmed nor refuted here.

BOTTOM LINE ON THE FIXED-LAYOUT HAZARD ITSELF: the structural hazards this protocol was chosen to test — the packed LI/VN/Mode octet, the fixed 48-byte layout, the total absence of length fields — are, for ENCODE, exactly where v0 does well. `bits` handles the packed octet; the fixed layout means the two-pass encoder, `len()`, and cyclic-span validation are never needed at all; capture A and capture B are byte-reproducible today. The grammar breaks on the DECODE side and on the CONVERTER side: it can write byte 0 but not read it, it can write a timestamp but never read one back, it has no fixed-point at all, and it cannot see past offset 48 because it cannot ask how many octets are left.

gaps.what: `bits` has no decode form, so the LI/VN/Mode octet cannot be parsed.
gaps.why: Byte 0 = 0x23 packs LI(2)|VN(3)|Mode(3). §3 defines `bits` as a list of slices each carrying `value`, and decode mode as "the same field list, fields carry `as:` instead of a value" — but a `bits` field has no top-level value to replace, and v0 never says where `as` goes on a slice or what path it binds. Mode is the field that decides whether the packet is a client request, a server reply, a symmetric peer packet, a broadcast, or a mode-6 control message with an entirely different header. v0 can encode byte 0 and cannot read it.

gaps.what: The whole `time` converter group is one-way: there is no inverse of `ntpTimestamp`, and `ntpTimestamp` has no declared width.
gaps.why: Offsets 16-47 carry four 64-bit NTP timestamps (32-bit seconds since 1900 + 32-bit binary fraction), e.g. ee22ea40 4ccccccd = 2026-08-09T12:00:00.300Z. Decode can only capture eight opaque u32be Ints; nothing in the closed converter set turns them into an instant, so a decoded NTP packet can never emit a time fact — which is the protocol's entire purpose. Compare hex/unhex, base64/unbase64, bcd/unbcd, dnsName/undnsName: every other group ships its inverse, `time` ships none. Separately, NTP has THREE timestamp formats (32-bit short 16.16 for root delay/dispersion, 64-bit 32.32 for the four timestamps, 128-bit date format) and v0 offers one unwidthed converter name.
gaps.proposedFix:
Replace `ntpTimestamp` with an explicit, paired, widthed set:
  ntp32 / unntp32     Instant <-> 4 bytes (NTP short, 16.16 seconds)
  ntp64 / unntp64     Instant <-> 8 bytes (32.32)
  ntp128 / unntp128   Instant <-> 16 bytes (NTP date format)
Usage: { "value":"now.utc | ntp64" } and { "bytes":8, "as":"txTs" } then "capture.txTs | unntp64". Make the same pairing rule a validation invariant: every wire-format converter must declare its inverse or be flagged decode-hostile at document-validate time.

gaps.what: No fixed-point converter, so 16.16 and 32.32 fields must be faked as pairs of integers.
gaps.why: Offsets 4-7 (root delay) and 8-11 (root dispersion) are NTP short format: a 32-bit value with the binary point between bits 15 and 16. 0x0000028f means 0.0099945068 s. v0 has u16be/u32be/i16be/i32be and no scaling, so the only way to hit those bytes is { "u16be":"0" },{ "u16be":"655" } — which makes the document's input "655 sixty-five-thousand-five-hundred-thirty-sixths of a second", a restatement of the wire format rather than an input. Decode is worse: two Ints that cannot be recombined. This also hides a genuine signedness fork: RFC 1305 §3.2 defines Root Delay as SIGNED 16.16; RFC 5905 §6 defines NTP short format as unsigned; real implementations emit negative root delays.
gaps.proposedFix:
Add a parameterised, paired fixed-point converter:
  fixed(intBits, fracBits, signed)   Number -> Bytes
  unfixed(intBits, fracBits, signed) Bytes  -> Number
Usage: { "u32be": "inputs.rootDelay | fixed(16,16,false)" } and
       { "bytes":4, "as":"rootDelayRaw" } -> "capture.rootDelayRaw | unfixed(16,16,false)".
This one converter also subsumes ntp32/ntp64 mantissas, Modbus scaled registers, BACnet, and IEEE 1588 correction fields.

gaps.what: No arithmetic in expressions — yet the decode example already uses infix `/`.
gaps.why: Three separate NTP requirements need it and none are reachable: (a) the 1900->1970 epoch offset, `now.utc | epochSeconds + 2208988800`; (b) the offset/delay computation theta = ((T2-T1)+(T3-T4))/2 and delta = (T4-T1)-(T3-T2), which is what `emits` would bind; (c) the Kiss-o'-Death backoff deadline now + 2^poll seconds. The converter table (§6) contains no add/sub/mul/div, yet §3's decode example writes "capture.byteCount / 2" — so infix arithmetic either exists undocumented or that example is invalid. Either way the precedence of `+`/`/` against the `|` pipeline operator is undefined, which makes `a | f + b` unparseable.
gaps.proposedFix: Document infix `+ - * / % << >> & | ^` with strictly LOWER precedence than the pipeline `|` operator (so `x | f + y` parses as `(x|f) + y`), and rename the pipeline operator to `|>` to remove the collision with bitwise-or. Alternatively, if infix is unwanted, add explicit converters add(n) sub(n) mul(n) div(n) mod(n) shl(n) shr(n) and DELETE the `capture.byteCount / 2` example, which currently advertises a feature the grammar does not have.

gaps.what: No raw-bytes capture field in decode mode.
gaps.why: Offsets 12-15 (reference id) and, in capture C, offsets 52-67 (the 16-byte MD5 digest) must be captured as opaque octets. v0's decode fields are: scalars (max 64 bits, produce Int), `skip` (discards), `each` (repetition), `tlv`/`tlvList`. The `{ "value": …, "repeat": n }` form is encode-only. So a 16-byte digest can only be captured as two u64be Ints, and a 4-byte refid as one u32be Int — which destroys the ASCII reading ("RATE" becomes 1381059397) and forces the comparison against a computed digest to happen in integer space.
gaps.proposedFix:
Add a first-class byte-span field, valid in both modes:
  encode: { "bytes": 16, "value": "<expr>" }        // width-checked at validate time
  decode: { "bytes": 16, "as": "macMd5" }
  decode: { "bytes": "remaining()", "as": "tail" }  // with G7
Produces a Bytes ProtoValue so the existing bytes-group converters (slice, xor, len, reverse) and any new un* converters apply directly.

gaps.what: A keyed digest whose key is an external prefix — not HMAC, not a plain span checksum — cannot be expressed, so NTP symmetric-key authentication is unreachable.
gaps.why: Capture C offsets 52-67 are MD5( ascii("secret") || bytes[0..48) ) = 7f7655604e4230124aa5396825317fe0. Four independent defeats: (1) `checksum.over` accepts only spans inside the message ("from:start to:here"), and the key is never on the wire, so there is no way to prepend it; (2) `hmacSha256(k)` is the wrong construction — RFC 5905 App.A specifies a prefix-MAC, hash(key||msg), which is NOT HMAC and NOT SHA-256; (3) there is no expression yielding the BYTES of a declared group — `len(group:X)` exists, `bytes(group:X)` does not — so the manual pipeline `consts.macKey | ascii | concat(bytes(group:ntpHeader)) | md5` is dead; (4) `checksum.as` is documented as a scalar name ("u16le") with no spelling for a 16-byte result.
gaps.proposedFix:
Two small, orthogonal additions. (a) Give `checksum` a key affix and a byte-width result:
  { "checksum": { "alg":"md5", "prefix":"consts.macKey | ascii",
                  "over":"from:start to:here", "as":"bytes:16" } }
  (also allow "suffix" — several protocols append the key instead.)
(b) Add the general escape so this never needs another special case: a span-bytes expression `bytes(group:X)` / `bytes(from:A to:B)`, alongside the existing `len(...)`, resolved in encode pass 2 exactly like `len`. With (b), (a) becomes sugar rather than a primitive.

gaps.what: No `remaining()` / datagram-length primitive, so the trailing region of a real NTP datagram is undecodable.
gaps.why: NTPv4 has NO length field anywhere. A datagram on :123 is 48 bytes (plain), 52 (crypto-NAK: key id 0, no digest — the server telling you your key is wrong), 68 (capture C: key id + MD5), 72 (key id + SHA-1), or 48 + extension fields (RFC 7822 TLVs, minimum length 28) optionally followed by a MAC. The receiver disambiguates purely by total length: `remaining = udpLen - 48`. v0's span expressions — len(group:X), len(after:X), len(from:A to:B) — all measure spans the DOCUMENT declared; none can ask the transport how many octets are actually left. Without it, decode simply stops at offset 48 and silently ignores authentication, which is a security failure, not a cosmetic one.
gaps.proposedFix:
Add two transport-provided span expressions usable in `when`, in `each` counts, and in the `bytes` width from G5:
  remaining()      // octets left in this layer's payload, at this field position
  len(datagram)    // total octets of this layer's payload
Both are decode-only and validate-time-typed as Int. Encode-side they are a validation error (there is no "rest" while building). This single primitive also unlocks DNS additional-records, CoAP payload marker handling, and every "read to end of PDU" protocol.

gaps.what: Decode `when` is not specified to see captures bound earlier in the same message — so the stratum-discriminated Reference ID cannot be interpreted.
gaps.why: Bytes 12-15 = 81 06 0f 1c. Their meaning depends on byte 1 (stratum), decoded eleven bytes earlier: stratum 0 -> 4-char ASCII kiss code ("RATE","DENY","RSTR","INIT"); stratum 1 -> ASCII source id ("GPS\0","PPS\0","DCF\0"); stratum >= 2 -> IPv4 address, or the first 4 bytes of MD5(IPv6). §3 gives `when` on a field but only ever illustrates it with `inputs.*` on the encode side, and §5 lists "no decoder-carried state" as an OPEN gap. This confirms that gap in its mildest form — the width is fixed at 4, only the interpretation varies — which means the fix is much cheaper than the CoAP-option-delta case that motivated the gap entry. Signedness of root delay (RFC 1305 vs 5905) is the same shape, keyed on capture.vn.
gaps.proposedFix:
Two parts. (1) Spec guarantee: decode binds fields strictly left-to-right and a field's `when` MAY reference any capture already bound in this message; forward references are a validate-time error (the dependency graph is already checked for cycles by the encode two-pass, so reuse that checker). (2) A zero-width `derive` field so reinterpretation needs no re-read:
  { "bytes":4, "as":"refIdRaw" },
  { "derive":"capture.refIdRaw | unascii", "as":"kissCode",   "when":"capture.stratum == 0" },
  { "derive":"capture.refIdRaw | unipv4",  "as":"upstreamIp", "when":"capture.stratum >= 2" }
Smaller than a `variant` field kind and generalises to every discriminated-interpretation field.

gaps.what: No late-bound field: T1 must be sampled at socket-write, and T4 (local receive instant) is not in the packet at all.
gaps.why: NTP measures the network, so the timestamps must bracket the actual syscalls. If offset 40-47 is filled during template encoding, every millisecond spent building the packet, traversing the socket buffer and reaching the NIC is folded into the measured offset — the encoder manufactures the error the protocol exists to measure. Symmetrically, decode needs T4 = the instant the reply arrived locally, which appears NOWHERE in the 48 bytes; the four-timestamp equations theta = ((T2-T1)+(T3-T4))/2 and delta = (T4-T1)-(T3-T2) are unsolvable from `capture.*` alone. This is the inverse of the case §3's two-pass handles: not "a value depending on bytes not yet emitted", but a value depending on an EVENT that has not yet happened.
gaps.proposedFix:
(a) Encode: a field annotation deferring evaluation to the transport write path:
  { "bytes":8, "value":"now.utc | ntp64", "at":"transmit" }
`at:"transmit"` fields must be fixed-width and must not participate in any checksum/len span (validate-time check — note this correctly REJECTS a MAC over a late-bound field, which is exactly why RFC 5905 hardware timestamping is hard).
(b) Decode: expose transport metadata as first-class paths — `meta.rxUtc`, `meta.txUtc`, `meta.srcIp`, `meta.srcPort`, `meta.datagramLen` — so `emits` can compute theta/delta once G4 lands.

gaps.what: No dispatch-by-discriminator on decode: a `listen` on :123 cannot choose between mode 3/4, mode 5 broadcast, and mode 6 control (a completely different header).
gaps.why: Modes share one UDP port and one first octet. Mode 6 (NTP control, RFC 5905 App.B) replaces the 48-byte layout with a 12-byte header — R/E/M flags + 5-bit opcode, 16-bit sequence, 16-bit status, 16-bit association id, 16-bit offset, 16-bit count — followed by `count` data octets and 0-3 pad octets. Mode 7 (ntpdc private) is different again. v0 attaches exactly one `parse` block per message and selects the message from the step graph, so an inbound datagram whose kind is not known in advance has no home. This is the `listen` step kind's central use case.
gaps.proposedFix:
Allow a `parse` to be a discriminated switch over a peeked prefix:
  "parse": { "switch": { "on": "peek(u8,0) & 0x07",
                          "cases": { "3": {"$ref":"parse.ntpClient"},
                                     "4": {"$ref":"parse.ntpServer"},
                                     "6": {"$ref":"parse.ntpControl"} },
                          "default": {"$ref":"parse.unknown"} } }
Requires a `peek(kind, offset)` expression (non-consuming read) and G4's `&`. Cases are validated independently; the switch itself consumes nothing.

gaps.what: `token` correlation has no binding syntax, and decode has no assertion field — so the Origin-echo anti-spoof check cannot be declared.
gaps.why: Bytes 24-31 of the response are a verbatim echo of bytes 40-47 of the request. That echo is the ONLY thing binding a reply to a request: a client MUST reject any packet whose Origin != its own transmit timestamp, or it accepts off-path spoofs and stale replies. §4 names `token` correlation and cites Modbus txn / DNS txid / CoAP token / SNMP request-id — all small scalars in an obvious field — but gives no syntax for declaring WHICH field is the token, and NTP's is an 8-byte span that is partly a random nonce and must be remembered across the send/expect pair. Decode also has no assert primitive: there is no field form meaning "these bytes must equal <expr> or this packet is not mine".
gaps.proposedFix:
Declare correlation explicitly on the `expect` step, and give decode an equality assertion:
  { "id":"gotReply", "kind":"expect", "message":"ntpServerResponse",
    "correlate": { "kind":"token",
                   "local":"msg.ntpClientRequest | slice(40,8)",
                   "remote":"capture.originTsRaw",
                   "onMismatch":"drop" } }        // drop | error | match-edge
and, for in-parse use:
  { "bytes":8, "as":"originTsRaw", "equals":"state.t1Bytes", "onMismatch":"drop" }
`onMismatch:"drop"` (keep listening) is distinct from `"error"` (fail the step) — an important difference under a spoofing flood.

gaps.what: Kiss-o'-Death is protocol state that must persist and gate future sends, but `implies` can only set a state name and invalidate keys — it cannot write `store.*`, and no step can be gated on a deadline.
gaps.why: A response with stratum=0 and refid ASCII "RATE" means: you are polling too fast, increase your poll interval and back off — and the RATE kiss also carries the server's demanded poll in byte 2. "DENY" and "RSTR" mean stop contacting this server, permanently, from this address. These outcomes must survive the run (`state.*` is one run, `session.*` is one connection — NTP has no connection), so they belong in `store.*` (persisted per protocol+device), and they must PREVENT the next send rather than merely label a state. §5's `implies` offers only { when, state, invalidate }.
gaps.proposedFix:
Extend `implies` with a `set` map, and add a step-level precondition:
  { "kind":"expect", "implies": [
      { "when":"capture.stratum == 0 && capture.kissCode == 'RATE'",
        "set": { "store.minPollLog2":"max(store.minPollLog2, capture.pollLog2 + 1)",
                 "store.nextAllowedUtc":"now.utc + pow(2, capture.pollLog2)" } },
      { "when":"capture.stratum == 0 && (capture.kissCode == 'DENY' || capture.kissCode == 'RSTR')",
        "set": { "store.blacklisted": true } } ] }
  { "id":"send", "kind":"send", "gate":"!store.blacklisted && now.utc >= store.nextAllowedUtc",
    "onGateBlocked":"skip" }
This is the generic rate-limit/backoff primitive; it is not NTP-specific.

gaps.what: Negotiated capability confirmed, with a concrete instance: version downgrade and poll clamping.
gaps.why: §5's first known gap is real here and is NOT limited to MQTT SUBACK. Two instances in these 48 bytes: (1) VERSION — a client sends VN=4 (byte 0 = 0x23); a server that only speaks NTPv3 replies with VN=3 (byte 0 = 0x1c), and the client must accept it and downgrade subsequent requests. The response grants strictly less than requested, and the grant is encoded in the same bit-field that carried the request. (2) POLL — the client proposes poll=6 (byte 2 = 0x06); the server may return a different poll, and the client must clamp its own next interval into [minpoll, maxpoll] intersected with the server's demand. Both are stateful negotiations whose result must condition the NEXT encode, and v0 has no vocabulary for "the response's value replaces my input for future messages".

gaps.what: Presumed facts decay continuously; `effects.ttl` can only model a cliff.
gaps.why: After a successful exchange the clock offset is a presumed fact, but its uncertainty grows CONTINUOUSLY: RFC 5905 §11.2 has dispersion accumulate at PHI = 15 ppm per second since the last update, and the packet even carries the inputs — root dispersion (bytes 8-11) and reference timestamp (bytes 16-23) tell you where the decay starts and how big it already is. `"effects": { "confidence":"likely", "ttl":"PT30S" }` says the fact is fully trusted for 30 s and worthless at 30.001 s, which is the wrong shape for every measured-quantity fact (temperature, battery, RSSI, position — not just time).
gaps.proposedFix:
Give `effects` a decay function alongside `ttl`:
  "effects": { "presume": { "dev.time.offsetSeconds":"state.theta" },
               "confidence":"measured",
               "decay": { "kind":"linear", "ratePerSecond": 1.5e-5,
                          "base":"capture.rootDispersion",
                          "since":"capture.refTs",
                          "expiresWhen":"error > 0.128" } }
`kind` in { none, linear, exponential }; `ttl` remains as sugar for kind:none + a deadline.

gaps.what: NTP era rollover makes any bytes-to-instant converter impure — it needs the local clock as external context.
gaps.why: The 32-bit seconds field wraps every 136 years; era 0 ends 2036-02-07T06:28:16Z. Capture A's 0xee22ea40 = 3995265600 is unambiguous ONLY because we assume era 0. RFC 5905 §6 resolves the ambiguity by assuming the true time is within 68 years of the local clock — i.e. the decoder must consult state outside the packet. So the proposed `unntp64` is not a pure function of its 8 input bytes, which quietly contradicts the "one decoder, per-field fold" model and the §6 claim that converters are typed input->output functions.
gaps.proposedFix:
Make the era an explicit converter argument with a documented default, so the impurity is declared rather than hidden:
  unntp64(eraHint)   // eraHint defaults to now.utc; era = round((eraHint - decoded)/2^32)
  ntp64(era)         // era defaults to 0
and have the converter's declared kinds record the external dependency (kind: Bytes -> Instant, depends: [clock]) so document validation can warn when a decode is not reproducible from bytes alone.

gaps.what: The `udp` layer cannot request a bound source port, which NTP symmetric mode requires.
gaps.why: §2 says the udp layer 'emits payload; engine sets ports'. Client mode (capture A) is fine with an ephemeral source port. But NTP symmetric active/passive (modes 1/2) requires source port 123 as well as destination 123, because the peer correlates by 4-tuple and replies to the source; broadcast/multicast client mode (modes 5/6) likewise needs a bound :123 listener that both sends and receives on one socket. There is no way to say so.
gaps.proposedFix:
{ "kind":"udp", "srcPort":123, "dstPort":123, "bindSrc":true, "reuse":true }
with `bindSrc` a hard bind (fail the step if unavailable, rather than silently falling back to ephemeral — silent fallback would make symmetric mode fail in a way that only shows up as missing replies).
